239-я.finding: «239-я» is shorthand for St Petersburg's Presidential Physics and Mathematics Lyceum No. 239, founded 1918, which in 1961 became the USSR's first specialized math school (set up with the Steklov Institute, Zalgaller teaching). By the 2000s–2010s it was one of Russia's most selective and decorated elite schools — a pipeline of olympiad winners and future mathematicians and programmers — so for a Russian reader the bare number signified 'top-tier math-nerd institution'. Durov attending it marks him as part of that St Petersburg math-programming elite.
239-я.register: colloquial (Russian shorthand naming an elite institution)

rendering.en: the elite St Petersburg physics-and-mathematics Lyceum No. 239
rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡第239数学物理中学（当地顶尖理科中学）
rendering.ja: サンクトペテルブルクの物理数学系名門校第239中等学校

239-я.rationale: The bare-number shorthand is meaningless outside Russian, so all three renderings unpack the gloss and add the elite math-school connotation that the original carried implicitly; I sacrifice the terse colloquial register ('239-я') but keep denotation and prestige, which matter more for a business biography. The zh version adds a brief in-line apposition rather than a footnote per the brief.

239-я школа.finding: This is St Petersburg's Presidential Physics and Mathematics Lyceum No. 239 (Президентский физико-математический лицей № 239), founded 1918, one of the Soviet/Russian specialized physics-math schools (spetsshkola) that produced multiple International Mathematical Olympiad champions, Fields medalists such as Stanislav Smirnov and Grigori Perelman, and much of the city's technical elite. For a Russian reader in 2013 the bare number '239' instantly signals elite math schooling; Durov's attendance marks him as part of that high-IU technical culture. The number must be kept, and the physics-math specialization plus a prestige cue carried for readers without the Russian context.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/スタニスラフ・スミルノフ

rendering.en: the elite St Petersburg physics-and-mathematics school No. 239 (Perelman's alma mater)
rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡精英物理数学中学第239中学
rendering.ja: サンクトペテルブルクの名門・物理数学専門学校（リツェイ）第239校

239-я школа.rationale: I kept the number and the institution type in all three, and converted the Russian reader's instant prestige association into explicit signals ('elite', '名門', '精英') — Perelman is added for English as the concrete analogue since 'physics-math school No. 239' means nothing otherwise. I sacrificed brevity and the insider shorthand tone of the original '239-я школа'.

activist capitalism.finding: No Wikipedia article or established Russian, English, Chinese or Japanese lemma exists for «activist capitalism» / «активистский капитализм» as a named 2013 movement. In a reported biography of Pavel Durov it is a nonce English-style label for founders who treat a commercially built platform as a tool of civic or political leverage, not for hedge-fund shareholder activism. For a Russian reader around 2013 it carried a Silicon-Valley-libertarian, slightly manifesto-like flavour associated with Durov’s public stance against state pressure on VKontakte.

rendering.ja: アクティビスト・キャピタリズム

activist capitalism.rationale: Kept the coinage as a named movement (denotation and slightly elevated register) and avoided ‘shareholder activism’ / 株主アクティビズム. Sacrificed an explanatory paraphrase that would have made the civic-platform sense fully transparent without context.

Astrum.finding: Astrum Online Entertainment was a Russian IT holding company formed in 2008-2009 from a merger of Nival Online, IT Territory, and Time Zero, operating in the interactive online entertainment market of Eastern Europe. In 2009 it passed under Mail.ru Group's control (later becoming part of what is now My.Games). For a Russian reader circa 2013 the name signaled a corporate gaming conglomerate tied to Mail.ru, not a single game or social platform.

rendering.en: Astrum Online Entertainment, a gaming holding company
rendering.zh: Astrum Online Entertainment游戏控股公司
rendering.ja: ゲーム持株会社アストラム・オンライン・エンターテインメント

Astrum.rationale: Preserved denotation (it's a corporate holding, not a game) and register (neutral business biography tone) by spelling out 'holding company'; sacrificed the brevity of the bare name and any connotative resonance it may have had for contemporary Russian readers.

Businessweek.finding: Bloomberg Businessweek is an American business magazine founded in 1929 (as BusinessWeek, acquired and rebranded by Bloomberg in 2010). In a 2013 Russian text about Durov/VKontakte, a citation from it signals coverage by a top-tier, internationally respected Western business publication, lending prestige and credibility to claims about Durov's wealth, business decisions, or company valuation.

rendering.ja: 『ブルームバーグ・ビジネスウィーク』

Businessweek.rationale: Preserve denotation and register (formal, prestige business press) by using each language's standard established name for the outlet; connotation of authoritative Western business journalism carries over naturally via the full official name.

CityBuilder.finding: The reference is almost certainly to CityVille, Zynga's hugely popular Facebook city-building simulation game released December 2010, which alongside FarmVille was one of the flagship 'social games' that drove Facebook app platform traffic in the early 2010s. In the Russian biography the term is used generically ('CityBuilder') as shorthand for this genre of Zynga city-sim games rather than as a precise product title, signaling the broader social-gaming craze VKontakte/Facebook competed with or emulated. For a Russian reader circa 2013, it connoted the same casual, mass-market, slightly derided 'time-waster' Facebook game genre that FarmVille represented, used as a comparison point for VKontakte's own gaming ecosystem.

rendering.ja: シティビル(都市経営ゲーム)

CityBuilder.rationale: Preserves denotation by correcting to the actual game title (CityVille) while keeping the genre gloss so readers understand it as a Zynga city-builder comparable to FarmVille; sacrifices the original generic English phrasing 'CityBuilder' in favor of accuracy, since it likely refers to a real, identifiable product rather than a purely descriptive term.

«Деловой Петербург» / dp.ru.finding: «Деловой Петербург» was a Saint Petersburg-based Russian business newspaper founded in 1993, with dp.ru as its website. Around 2013 it was a weekday daily owned by Sweden’s Bonnier Business Press, publishing business news, analysis, investigations, and interviews; its distinctive pink paper evoked established international financial newspapers. For Russian readers, the name denoted a credible regional business publication rather than a generic description of Petersburg commerce.
«Деловой Петербург» / dp.ru.rationale: The English keeps the publication’s proper name and domain, while Chinese and Japanese use concise newspaper-style translations that preserve its business-press identity and local association. This sacrifices the Russian title’s exact wording and, in English, some immediate semantic transparency, but avoids mistaking dp.ru for a separate outlet.

DST.finding: DST refers to Digital Sky Technologies, Yuri Milner’s internet-investment company and VKontakte’s first outside institutional investor. It acquired 24.99% of VKontakte in 2007; in 2010 its Russian operating assets were renamed Mail.ru Group, while international investments continued separately through DST Global. For a Russian business reader around 2013, “DST” evoked Milner’s powerful, well-connected investment vehicle rather than an unexplained technical acronym.

rendering.ja: DST（デジタル・スカイ・テクノロジーズ）

DST.rationale: All three renderings preserve the historically used acronym and distinguish the entity from the later DST Global; spelling out the name supplies the context non-Russian readers lack. Chinese adds “投资集团” to preserve its business function, sacrificing some formal name exactness, while Japanese retains a sober corporate-biography register.

DST Deal.finding: This was not a formally named financial instrument but an industry label for the investment model associated with Yuri Milner’s Digital Sky Technologies: invest large sums in mature internet companies at generous valuations, accept a minority stake, leave founders in control, and use relatively simple terms. Around 2013, a Russian business reader would hear it as venture-capital jargon with approving connotations of founder-friendly, fast, nonintrusive money; the consulted Wikipedia articles confirm DST’s late-stage strategy and major minority investments but do not establish “DST Deal” as a standardized proper name.
DST Deal.rationale: These renderings preserve the reference to DST and signal a recognizable deal-making model rather than one particular transaction. English and Japanese sacrifice the source’s quasi-proper-name compactness for immediate clarity; Chinese retains the concise industry-label effect.

Forticom.finding: Forticom was a Riga-based Latvian IT company that operated the Baltic social networks One.lv and One.lt and invested in Odnoklassniki, acquiring a 25% stake in 2007. In the Odnoklassniki ownership structure, the Latvian company was affiliated with Forticom Group Ltd., a British Virgin Islands vehicle used for Yuri Milner’s DST investment. For a Russian business reader around 2013, the name therefore denoted a corporate owner and investment vehicle in the consolidation of major post-Soviet social networks, not a consumer brand and not Fortinet.
Forticom.rationale: The official Latin-script name is retained in all three languages, preserving exact corporate denotation; Chinese 公司 and Japanese 社 supply the institutional cue that the bare unfamiliar name lacks. This sacrifices none of the neutral business register, while the wider ownership implications must remain contextual rather than be built into the name.

Golden Dolls.finding: Golden Dolls is a strip club in central Saint Petersburg, a prominent fixture of the city's nightlife in the 2000s and early 2010s. It is referenced in accounts of Pavel Durov's VKontakte period, notably in memoirs and reporting about his flamboyant public events, such as throwing dollarbearing paper airplanes from the window of the VKontakte office during City Day in 2012—an episode tied in the Russian press to the club's name and to his public persona. For a Russian reader in 2013 the name connoted elite, expensive nightlife: a place of stage show, nudity, money, and proximity to wealthy or status-conscious men; it was part of a well-known striptease brand with clubs in Moscow and elsewhere. The name itself is an English-language brand (in Latin letters), so its Russian connotation is that of an imported, Westernised luxury vice rather than a purely local term. I could not confirm a standalone Russian Wikipedia article for the club; it appears in Russian media coverage and memoirs rather than as an indexed Wikipedia entry.
sources: Russian news coverage of Durov's May 2012 paperairplane stunt (e.g. Lenta, Fontanka, Komsomolskaya Pravda reports)

rendering.ja: ストリップクラブ「Golden Dolls」

Golden Dolls.rationale: For all three languages the decision preserves the Latin brand name, which Russian readers themselves encountered in Latin letters; English keeps it bare, Chinese keeps the Latin brand plus a gloss for readers who lack the stripclub context, and Japanese keeps Latin as the official brand with katakana-friendly context appended. In each case the denotation (a specific named club) is preserved; connotative suggestions of luxury and vice are lightly reinforced in zh and ja via the explicit '脱衣舞俱乐部'/'ストリップクラブ' gloss, which the original Russian could leave implicit.

HighLoad-2011.finding: HighLoad（后来的 HighLoad++）是俄罗斯规模最大的、面向高负载互联网/IT 系统开发者的专业会议，2007 年首次举办，每年在莫斯科举行。到 2013 年传记写作时，对一个俄罗斯技术读者来说，HighLoad-2011 指的就是其中 2011 年那一届会议，暗示 Durov/VKontakte 团队在大型并发系统这一严肃科技圈子里抛头露面、分享技术经验（VKontakte 是俄罗斯最著名的高负载站点之一）。该名称是一个专有活动名，而不是泛泛而谈的“人很多的会议”。
HighLoad-2011.rationale: 保留专名 HighLoad 2011 的指称（denotation）与活动氛围（科技行业集会），在英文里补上 conference 使无背景读者明白它是会议；中文、日文分别用“大会”“カンファレンス”给出可懂的面貌，牺牲了俄语圈特有的“HighLoad”作为圈内黑话的精确发音/品牌感。

HighLoad.finding: HighLoad (HighLoad++) is Russia's premier and longest-running professional conference for developers of high-load, large-scale systems, first held in 2007 and still run by the team behind the IT events company around Oleg Bunin. By 2013 it connoted the pinnacle of Russian backend/systems engineering expertise — a venue where senior engineers from VKontakte, Yandex, Mail.ru and Rambler presented scaling war stories. Pavel Durov himself spoke at the HighLoad++ conference in Moscow in 2010, and VKontakte's CTO regularly announced technical milestones there, so for a 2013 reader the name carried instant authority and prestige within the Runet engineering scene, not a generic 'high load' adjective.
HighLoad.rationale: I keep the recognized English-language proper name (denotation and register of the technical conference name) rather than translating it as a generic adjective, adding 大会 / カンファレンス where a bare acronym would be under-determined for the target reader; the trade-off is that the pun on high-load scaling is not explained for non-engineers.

id (первые id).finding: VKontakte assigned integer user IDs sequentially from launch in 2006 (Pavel Durov is id 1). In the mid-2000s–2013 Runet, a low number was a public badge of early membership, insider status and sometimes of being in Durov’s student/IT circle; people displayed and compared IDs the way early Facebook users did. The parenthetical «первые id» names that prestige, not a technical subtype of identifier.

rendering.zh: 用户ID（早期低号，越早注册越显身份）
rendering.ja: ユーザーID（初期の低番号＝古参の証）

id (первые id).rationale: Denotation (sequential numeric ID) and the prestige connotation of a low number are kept in a short parenthetical; register stays explanatory-biography rather than slang. Pure calque without the status note would lose what 2013 Russian readers heard.

id2, Александра Владимирова.finding: On VKontakte, account numbers (id1, id2, …) were assigned sequentially at registration in 2006, so a single-digit ID marks a founding-era account: id1 belongs to Pavel Durov himself, and id2 — the account of 'Александра Владимирова' — is the network's second-ever registered profile. In 2013 VK lore this was an insider badge of honour: the person holding id2 was understood as one of Durov's inner circle from the launch, reportedly taking on user-support duties in the early days. Wikipedia has no dedicated article on her; the identity rests on the 2013 Durov biography and VK's own id-numbering convention, which is verifiable (profile URLs are vk.com/id1, vk.com/id2).
sources: vk.com/id2 (profile URL confirming the id-numbering scheme)

rendering.en: Alexandra Vladimirova — the network's second-ever registered user, holding account ID2, who took over early user support
rendering.zh: 第二号用户（ID2）亚历山德拉·弗拉基米洛娃——注册编号仅次于杜罗夫的元老账号，早期负责客服
rendering.ja: VKの第2号ユーザー（ID2）アレクサンドラ・ヴラジーミロヴァ——デュロフに次いで登録された初期メンバーで、初期のユーザーサポートを担当した

id2, Александра Владимирова.rationale: All three renderings add a short in-line gloss ('second-ever registered user') so the low-ID badge of founding-era status is legible without a footnote, while the ID2 numeral itself and the transliterated name preserve the denotation exactly; what is sacrificed is the untranslated 'id2' shorthand and any hint about the folklore aura around who Alexandra really was, which cannot be carried concisely.

Le Web.finding: LeWeb (stylized Le Web in the Russian text) is the annual technology and internet conference founded in Paris in 2004 by French entrepreneurs Loïc and Géraldine Le Meur; by the early 2010s it drew several thousand attendees from dozens of countries and was routinely described as Europe's premier web industry gathering. For a Russian reader around 2013 it connoted the prestigious European tech-elite stage — the Russian press covered Durov's appearances there as a sign VKontakte had international standing. Calling it a 'festival' (фестиваль) was loose Russian journalistic labeling of a conference, not an arts event.
sources: ru.wikipedia.org search confirming Russian press usage «конференция LeWeb»

rendering.ja: 欧州最大級のテクノロジーカンファレンスLeWeb

Le Web.rationale: I preserved denotation (a tech industry conference, not an arts festival) and the prestige connotation by adding a descriptor in each language; I sacrificed the original's 'festival' label, which in all three target languages would wrongly suggest a cultural event. The zh proposal is confirmed as correct; ja gains a status cue befitting a serious business biography.

Livejournal.finding: LiveJournal (Russian: Живой Журнал, «ЖЖ») is a blogging and social-networking platform founded in 1999 by Brad Fitzpatrick; sold to Six Apart in 2005 and to the Russian company SUP Media in 2007. By 2013 it was the central hub of Russian internet culture — the de facto public square of the Runet, hosting bloggers, journalists, opposition figures (Navalny), and even Medvedev's official blog, and functioning as Russia's largest online community (roughly half its traffic came from Russia). Its one-way 'friending' model and 'friends feed' made it a social network avant la lettre. For a Russian reader of 2013, 'ЖЖ' connoted not just a platform but an entire era and ecosystem of Russian online discourse.
Livejournal.rationale: The brand name is identical across languages and is the established form in each Wikipedia edition, so denotation and register are fully preserved by keeping the proper noun; Japanese convention uses katakana ライブジャーナル, with the Latin form on first mention for a serious business biography. What is inevitably lost for en/zh/ja readers is the connotative weight — LiveJournal as the Russian-speaking internet's public square — which no rendering can carry and which surrounding context must supply.

Mafия (игра «Мафия»).finding: «Мафия» is the social-deduction party game invented in 1986 by Moscow State University psychology student Dmitry Davidoff; by the 2000s–2013 it was a ubiquitous club and office pastime in Russia, with organized clubs and even a federation. Players are secretly split into an informed minority (the mafia) and an uninformed majority (townspeople) who debate and vote each round to eliminate suspects — so as a metaphor for a boardroom purge it evokes hidden loyalties, denunciation by vote, and ritual elimination, not literal organized crime. In English the game is known as Mafia or Werewolf; in China the direct descendant is 杀人游戏 ('killer game'), the precursor of 狼人杀; in Japan the culturally dominant analogue is 人狼ゲーム (Jinro/werewolf game), though マフィアゲーム is also understood.
Mafия (игра «Мафия»).rationale: All three renderings keep the word Mafia (preserving the Russian term and the sly mafia-in-the-boardroom pun) while anchoring it as the game: English needs only 'a game of' since Mafia is known; Chinese pairs the native analogue 杀人游戏 with the original name; Japanese glosses with 人狼ゲーム so business-biography readers recognize the genre. Sacrificed: the exact Russian flavor of dorm-room клубная игра culture, traded for instant recognizability of the elimination-by-vote metaphor.

Mail.ru.finding: Mail.ru Group (originally Digital Sky Technologies, renamed VK in October 2021) was the Russian internet holding that acquired a controlling stake in VKontakte between 2011 and 2014. In 2011, when the holding attempted a full buyout to merge VKontakte with Odnoklassniki, Durov publicly called it a 'трэш-холдинг' (trash holding). For a Russian reader around 2013, 'Mail.ru' was universally recognized as the corporate name; the brand was ubiquitous in the Russian internet space. The 'трэш-холдинг' epithet was Durov's own coinage expressing contempt for the holding's aggressive tactics. All three language editions of Wikipedia use the Latin form 'Mail.ru' or 'Mail.ru Group' without transliteration.
Mail.ru.rationale: The name is a proper noun / brand written in Latin script in all languages; preserving the original form maintains denotation and period accuracy. The connotation of the 'трэш-холдинг' insult is a separate translation issue handled at the phrase level, not at the org-name level; the org name itself stays neutral. Nothing is sacrificed for denotation or register; the only loss is that a reader unfamiliar with Russian internet history gets no contextual signal from the name itself, which is acceptable.

Mail.ru Group.finding: Mail.ru Group was the Russian Internet holding and investment company that, until its October 2021 rebranding to VK, was the corporate vehicle through which Yuri Milner's Digital Sky Technologies (DST) was folded into the Mail.ru business. In September 2010 DST was renamed Mail.ru Group, and its CEO/co-founder was Dmitry Grishin (who had headed Mail.ru since 2001). By 2013 Mail.ru Group held the controlling stakes in Russia's two leading social networks, VKontakte and Odnoklassniki, and in 2014 it took full control of VKontakte after Pavel Durov's departure. So for a 2013 Russian reader the name signalled the dominant consolidated Internet holding—owning the Mail.ru email/portal plus both big social networks—rather than merely the email service itself.
Mail.ru Group.rationale: The brand is the entity's proper name and already circulates in the Latin script in all three target languages; adding the local generic for 'Group' (集团 / グループ) preserves register and denotation while keeping the Latin brand intact, avoiding an inconsistent Greek-style transliteration like Mail.ru吉集团. Register (formal corporate name) and denotation are preserved; the local generic is a near-identity rather than an exact lexical match.

MoiFacultet.finding: MoiFacultet (МойФакультет, 'My Faculty') was a small Russian student-oriented social network active in the mid-to-late 2000s, one of several niche competitors to VKontakte during its early growth. No Wikipedia article exists in any language edition consulted (ru, en, ja, zh), and no detailed independent source was located via available searches. The name is a Latin-script transliteration of the Russian phrase 'Мой факультет,' following the common Russian-internet convention of rendering domain names in transliterated Russian. For a 2013 Russian reader it would have been recognizable as a minor, largely forgotten student-networking site that lost to VKontakte.
MoiFacultet.rationale: The transliterated form is preserved as the proper name in all three languages since no established localized equivalent exists in any target-language source. A brief gloss in parentheses is added for zh and ja readers who cannot parse the Russian-origin transliteration, sacrificing some concision for comprehensibility. In English the name is left unglossed because the surrounding context of the biography makes the student-networking function clear.

MoiFakultet.ru / MoiFacultet.finding: MoiFakultet.ru was a small student-oriented social network associated with Moscow State University (МГУ), launched in the mid-2000s as a direct competitor to VKontakte in its early days. It is mentioned in the 2013 biography 'Код Дурова' by Nikolai Kononov as one of the early rivals VK faced. The spelling inconsistency in the source (Fakultet vs. Facultet) reflects the ambiguity between Russian transliteration (факультет → fakultet) and the English loanword spelling (faculty → facultet). The site no longer exists and has no Wikipedia article in any language; it is known only from secondary sources about VK's history. The correct Russian word is 'факультет', which transliterates as 'fakultet' in standard romanization.
MoiFakultet.ru / MoiFacultet.rationale: Preserved the domain name as a proper noun in Latin script, normalizing to 'Fakultet' (the standard transliteration of факультет). No translation or gloss is added because the name functions purely as a brand/domain; connotation of 'my faculty' is self-evident to Russian readers but adding a gloss in translation would over-explain a minor historical competitor. The .ru suffix is kept to signal it was a Russian web project.

Nginx.finding: Nginx (pronounced 'engine-x') is a high-performance open-source HTTP server and reverse proxy created by Russian developer Igor Sysoev, first released in 2004 while he worked at Rambler. By 2013, it had become the standard infrastructure powering the world's highest-traffic websites, including VKontakte, Rambler, and Yandex, serving as a massive source of domestic pride in the Russian tech industry as one of its most globally successful engineering exports.
Nginx.rationale: Preserved the universally recognized international technical brand name and trademark across all three languages without phonetic transliteration, sacrificing explicit explanation of its Russian origin since technical readers recognize it immediately and general context conveys its role.

res publica.finding: Latin for 'the public thing/affair' — the commonwealth or public realm held in common by citizens, originally opposed to res privata. In the 2013 Russian context the author uses it in the Arendtian sense: the political sphere created and sustained by citizens' participation, not the form-of-government 'republic' the word later became. Russian Wikipedia likewise distinguishes the etymon ('общее дело', public property, public realm) from the modern 'республика' that descended from it via French république. So the reference is to VKontakte as a self-governing public space, not to a state form.

rendering.zh: 公共事务（拉丁语 res publica）
rendering.ja: レス・プブリカ（公共的領域）

res publica.rationale: English keeps the Latin with a brief appositive, preserving the Arendtian 'public realm' denotation while the Latin gives the learned register of the original; Chinese leads with a native term so readers grasp the concept at first sight and brackets the Latin to signal the classical reference it invokes; Japanese keeps the katakana Latin plus gloss already current in Japanese Arendt scholarship, matching a serious business-biography register. All three sacrifice any echo of the modern 'republic' reading, which is exactly the misreading to avoid.

Roem.ru.finding: Founded in late 2007 by Yuri Sinodov and co-owned with Igor Ashmanov, Roem.ru was the premier specialized news and industry-insider portal for the Russian internet industry (Runet). Unlike general tech blogs, it was structured around industry scoops, insider leaks, and blunt direct debates in the comments between IT executives, founders, and community members, functioning as Runet's primary industry watering hole in the late 2000s and early 2010s.

rendering.zh: 俄罗斯互联网行业媒体 Roem.ru
rendering.ja: ロシアのIT業界ニュースサイト「Roem.ru」

Roem.ru.rationale: Preserves the distinct domain brand name while glossing its specific status as the central RuNet IT industry media outlet so readers understand it is a professional trade/industry platform rather than an anonymous social network or generic forum.

so long, and thanks for all the fish («А.term: so long, and thanks for all the fish («Автостопом по галактике»)
so long, and thanks for all the fish («А.finding: The line is the dolphins' farewell message to humanity in Douglas Adams' Hitchhiker's Guide series, and the title of the fourth book; in Russian it circulated widely as «Всего доброго, и спасибо за рыбку» from the «Автостопом по галактике» series, a cult text among Russian tech-minded readers of the 1990s–2000s. Used by the narrator, it is an ironic, affectionate sign-off — a wink that says 'I'm out of here, it's been fun' — rather than a literal goodbye. Around 2013 it also evoked Durov's own flair for geek references and abrupt exits. The Russian edition's exact wording could not be re-confirmed in this session's searches, but the series title «Автостопом по галактике» is confirmed on ru.wikipedia.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/銀河ヒッチハイク・ガイド

rendering.en: So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy)
rendering.zh: 《再见，谢谢鱼》（《银河系漫游指南》系列第四部书名，海豚向人类的告别语）
rendering.ja: 『さようなら、いままで魚をありがとう』（『銀河ヒッチハイク・ガイド』）

so long, and thanks for all the fish («А.rationale: Keeps the localized book-title wording each market already knows (Japanese Kawade bunko title; mainland Chinese 《再见，谢谢鱼》), so the irony and recognition are preserved; the English original needs no change. Zh adds a minimal in-text gloss because the dolphin line is less universally recognized there; sacrifice is brevity in zh, and the ja rendering forgoes an explanatory note as the Kawade editions are well known to the SF-reading audience.

spbgu.org.finding: This refers to an unofficial student web forum created by Pavel Durov while at St. Petersburg State University (SPbSU), distinct from the university's official domain (spbu.ru). Sources vary between 'spbgu.ru' and 'spbgu.org' as the forum's address, but both denote the same informal, student-run community site that predates VKontakte and served as a proving ground for Durov's ideas about student social networking. For a Russian reader circa 2013, the domain signaled grassroots, unofficial, insider student culture — not an institutional resource.

rendering.zh: spbgu.org（杜罗夫创办的非官方学生论坛）
rendering.ja: spbgu.org（ドゥーロフが作った非公式の学生フォーラム）

spbgu.org.rationale: Preserved the literal domain (denotation) while adding a brief gloss to prevent confusion with the official university site and to carry the connotation of 'unofficial/grassroots' for readers unfamiliar with Russian student internet culture; sacrificed brevity/register neutrality for clarity.

Spbgu.ru.finding: Spbgu.ru was an unofficial student forum for St. Petersburg State University created by Pavel Durov during his studies in the early-to-mid 2000s, which served as his testing ground for community moderation, anonymous identity experiments, and campus popularity contests. It was the direct technological and conceptual precursor to VKontakte. Later, disputes over the official university name and domain ownership led to transitions involving spbgu.org, making exact domain preservation critical to tracking the platform's history.
Spbgu.ru.rationale: Preserves verbatim domain accuracy across all languages to cleanly distinguish it from the later spbgu.org, while appending '学生论坛' in Chinese so general readers immediately grasp the campus BBS nature of early-2000s Russian web culture without requiring a footnote.

«Афиша».finding: «Афиша» was a Moscow-based print magazine launched in 1999 covering city entertainment, culture, restaurants and nightlife; it became a trend-setting urban lifestyle/culture guide for the young educated Moscow reader, analogous in cultural niche to Time Out. By the 2010s it merged into Rambler and later became a primarily online publication (Rambler-Afisha). For a Russian reader in 2013 it signaled hip, up-to-date urban culture journalism, not a literal 'poster/bill'.

rendering.en: Afisha (a Moscow culture/listings magazine, akin to Time Out)
rendering.zh: 《Afisha》（莫斯科文化生活杂志，类似《Time Out》）
rendering.ja: 『アフィシャ』（モスクワの都市文化情報誌）

«Афиша».rationale: Preserved denotation (proper name, transliterated) and added a brief functional gloss to carry connotation (urban culture magazine) for readers unfamiliar with Russian media landscape; sacrificed the literal meaning of the word itself since it functions purely as a brand name.

«ВКадре».finding: «ВКадре» was VKontakte's in-house video-hosting service (literally 'In Frame'/'In Shot'), built by developer Oleg Andreev as VK's answer to YouTube, letting users upload and watch video directly on the VK platform. The name puns on 'В Контакте' (VKontakte) prefix 'В-' plus 'кадр' (film frame/shot), signaling it as VK's native, integrated video product rather than a third-party embed. For Russian readers circa 2013 it connoted VK's drive toward media self-sufficiency and its playful naming convention shared with other VK sub-products.

rendering.zh: VKadre（VK内置视频平台，直译“入镜”）
rendering.ja: VKadre(VK社内製動画プラットフォーム)

«ВКадре».rationale: Kept the established transliteration used by other translators for consistency and denotation, sacrificing the internal pun ('в кадре' = 'in frame') by adding a brief functional gloss instead of a translated pun, since no natural equivalent preserves both sound and meaning.

дом Зингера.finding: Дом компании «Зингер» (Nevsky Prospekt 28, St Petersburg) is the 1902–1904 Art Nouveau headquarters of the Singer sewing-machine company, designed by Pavel Suzor; after nationalization it became the city’s famous Дом книги (House of the Book). For a 2013 Russian reader the name evokes a landmark office block on Nevsky, not a vocalist’s dwelling; VKontakte rented space there in the startup years, so it also signals a prestigious, slightly theatrical Petersburg address.
дом Зингера.rationale: Preserved the sewing-machine brand (Singer / 胜家 / シンガー) and the conventional building nickname so no reader hears ‘a singer’s house’; sacrificed the later local nickname Дом книги and the full ‘company house’ legal form.

Слава.finding: Refers to Vyacheslav (Yitzchak) Mirilashvili (born 1984), co-founder and initial majority shareholder of VKontakte, and son of prominent billionaire Mikhail Mirilashvili. In Russian conversational and narrative contexts regarding the founding circle of VK, close associates and colleagues regularly referred to him by his everyday hypocoristic 'Слава' rather than his formal given name 'Вячеслав'.
Слава.rationale: Preserved the informal familiarity of the Russian diminutive for narrative flow across all three target languages (Slava / 斯拉瓦 / スラヴァ); in contexts where introducing him initially in formal business prose is required, full names with 'Slava' in apposition may be preferred, but standalone 'Slava' matches the personal register of the source text.

«Герой Нашего Времени».finding: Это название социально-психологического романа Михаила Лермонтова «Герой нашего времени», написанного в 1837–1839 годах и впервые изданного в 1840 году. Для русского читателя 2013 года это легко узнаваемая отсылка к школьной классике и к Печорину — одарённому, отчуждённому, циничному байроническому антигерою и типу «лишнего человека». Необычная капитализация всех знаменательных слов усиливает эффект ярлыка: современного человека называют «героем эпохи» одновременно возвышенно и иронически.
«Герой Нашего Времени».rationale: Во всех трёх языках сохранены канонические названия романа, а кавычки книжного заглавия поддерживают литературную аллюзию. Ирония и печоринский оттенок антигероя могут быть слабее для читателя без знакомства с романом, но замена названием-«аналогом» уничтожила бы точную культурную отсылку.

Бунин.finding: In context of a 2013 VKontakte biography this is Oleg Vladimirovich Bunin, a well-known Russian web engineer and entrepreneur: lead developer at Rambler in the 2000s, later CTO of Badoo, and founder/organizer of HighLoad++, the flagship Russian conference on high-load web systems. To a 2013 Russian IT reader the bare surname «Бунин» signaled an insider, one of the 'elders' of the Runet engineering scene, not the Nobel laureate Ivan Bunin. There is no dedicated Wikipedia article on him, but the HighLoad++ connection is attested on ru.wikipedia (Igor Sysoev's talks at HighLoad++) and on the conference's own site.

rendering.en: Oleg Bunin, founder of the HighLoad++ conference
rendering.zh: 奥列格·布宁（Oleg Bunin，HighLoad++大会创办人）
rendering.ja: オレグ・ブーニン（HighLoad++カンファレンス創設者）

Бунин.rationale: Keeps the denotation (the person) and adds minimal identification so the reader does not default to Ivan Bunin; sacrifices the Russian insider cue carried by the bare surname, which cannot survive translation without expansion.

Равдоникас.finding: Refers to Ilya Ravdonikas (Илья Равдоникас), an early VKontakte team member, poet, copywriter, and close university associate of Pavel Durov who helped author text interfaces, public relations materials, and internal lore. The surname itself is of Lithuanian origin (Raudonikis/Ravdonikas, notable in St. Petersburg through archaeologist Vladislav Ravdonikas and musicologist Felix Ravdonikas). In the context of the 2013 book 'The Durov Code', the name functions strictly as an individual proper surname identifying a key creative figure in Durov's inner circle.
Равдоникас.rationale: Preserves standard biographical phonological transliteration of the rare Baltic/Russian surname across all target languages, maintaining consistency across chapters while sacrificing any semantic etymological transparency.

тотем.finding: Around 2010–2013 in VK office lore and Russian tech press, Pavel Durov was mock-reverently nicknamed «тотем»: employees and reporters treated the founder as a tribal totem—the sacred, slightly absurd clan-chief whose image, edicts and presence organized the tribe. It is not a legal title or a brand, but ironic cult-of-personality slang built on the ordinary anthropological word тотем. Wikipedia biographies do not record the nickname; the sense is carried by period journalism and insider talk, not by an encyclopedia lemma.
тотем.rationale: Kept the shared anthropological loanword so the mock-sacred clan-chief joke remains visible without a footnote; sacrificed extra gloss (e.g. ‘sacred founder’) because the irony already lives in calling a startup CEO a totem.

«Мой Мир».finding: Мой Мир (originally «Мой Мир@Mail.ru») is Mail.ru Group's Russian-language social network, launched from beta in August 2007 as an umbrella for the portal's blogs, video, photo and Answers services. Around 2013 it was VKontakte's principal domestic branded competitor, with a largely older/portal-loyal audience, and its name literally means 'My World.' English-language Wikipedia renders it 'Moy Mir (My World)', Japanese Mail.ru material uses 'モイミール', and Chinese material has used 'Moy Mir（我的世界）'.

rendering.zh: Moy Mir（Mail.ru 旗下社交网站“我的世界”）

«Мой Мир».rationale: Preserves denotation (a specific branded, competing social network) and the connotation of a proper competitor by keeping the transliterated brand name with a sourced gloss; sacrifices a literal rendering alone, which would hide that it is a product and—in Chinese—would collide with Minecraft's official name 我的世界.

«ВКонтакте».finding: «ВКонтакте» (international name VK) is the Russian social network Pavel Durov launched in 2006 in St. Petersburg, named from the slogan «В полном контакте с информацией» ('in full contact with information'); by 2013 it was Russia's largest social network, the 'Russian Facebook' analogue, central to a whole generation's online identity. Internationally it was known by its full brand VKontakte, with VK already used as a short form; in Japanese media it is usually transliterated フコンタクテ, and Chinese Wikipedia renders it as VKontakte. The name is a proper brand, so all renderings must preserve the denotation (this specific company) while the transliterated Russian flavor is less recoverable in CJK scripts.
«ВКонтакте».rationale: For English I keep the familiar brand VKontakte (the name under which the company was internationally known in 2013, with VK only as an abbreviation); for Chinese and Japanese I retain the official Latin brand VKontakte and supply the audience's own clue — VK for Chinese, the katakana reading フコンタクテ for Japanese — sacrificing only the Russian spelling/pronunciation flavor, which is unrecoverable in CJK script.

Дуров.finding: The surname of Pavel Durov (Павел Валерьевич Дуров, b. 1984), founder and CEO of VKontakte who by 2013 was one of Russia's most famous tech figures, dubbed 'Russia's Mark Zuckerberg' and known for libertarian views, eccentric gestures, and escalating conflict with the authorities over user data. For a 2013 Russian reader the bare surname functioned as a household name connoting the rebel-founder persona (the biography 'Код Дурова' had already appeared in 2012). All four Wikipedias consulted render the name by fixed transliteration: ru 'Дуров', en 'Durov', zh '杜罗夫' (simplified; traditional 杜洛夫), ja 'ドゥーロフ' (article title パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ; the shorter ドゥロフ also occurs in body text but the title settles the long vowels). The bare surname is technically shared with his brother Nikolai, but in this biography it denotes Pavel, and the ambiguity is preserved identically in every target language.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ
Дуров.rationale: Denotation (the specific person) and register (neutral surname mention) are fully preserved via each language's established transliteration; the celebrity-rebel connotation survives because by 2013 the transliterated name was already recognizable in all three target cultures. The only sacrifice is the Russian form's morphological masculinity marking, which zh/ja renderings cannot encode anyway.

филфак.finding: Colloquial abbreviation of the Philology Faculty (филологический факультет) of St Petersburg State University, where Pavel Durov enrolled in 2001 and where his VK project began among philology students. Russian 'филология' covers both linguistics and literature, and the SPbGU faculty teaches languages, linguistics, and literary studies; around 2007–2010 it was even briefly renamed 'Faculty of Philology and Arts' before an arts faculty split off in 2010. For a Russian reader 'филфак' carries a student, ironic register — the classic 'non-technical, humanities' faculty — and the abbreviation itself signals campus slang, not the official name.
sources: https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Код_Дурова (novel about Durov, 'студент филфака СПбГУ Павел Дуров')

rendering.en: the philology faculty (of St Petersburg State University)
rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡国立大学语文系
rendering.ja: サンクトペテルブルク大学文学部

филфак.rationale: In all three languages I preserve the denotation as a faculty-level unit covering both language and literature, rejecting the 'linguistics-only' reading of the proposed Japanese 言語学部 (Russian philology is conventionally 文学部 in Japanese for Soviet/Russian universities, and 语文系 is the established Chinese term for Russian филфак). The colloquial register of 'филфак' is sacrificed to the denotation, since a slangy abbreviation (e.g. English 'Phil Faculty') would be opaque and costlier than the small informality lost.

Сурков.finding: Vladislav Surkov was the Kremlin's chief ideologue and political strategist from 1999 to late 2011 (as First Deputy Chief of Staff), and later Deputy Prime Minister and presidential aide. Around 2013, the name 'Surkov' was shorthand in Russian political and media circles for the Kremlin's 'grey cardinal' who architected 'sovereign democracy', managed media agendas, co-opted youth and internet movements, and pulled strings behind Russian public discourse. For Durov's biography, mentioning Surkov evokes the subtle, psychological state-curation of the Russian tech and media landscape before heavy-handed security services (siloviki) took over.

rendering.en: Vladislav Surkov, the Kremlin's domestic policy chief
rendering.ja: クレムリンの世論工作を取り仕切るウラジスラフ・スルコフ
rendering.zh: 克里姆林宫主管舆论意识形态的“灰衣主教”苏尔科夫

Сурков.rationale: A bare surname leaves foreign readers clueless about the immense cultural-political weight he carried in 2013, so each rendering adds an appositive characterizing his role as Kremlin media/ideology puppetmaster ('grey cardinal' in Chinese, policy chief in English and Japanese), sacrificing brevity to preserve the political stakes of Durov's interactions with power.

«Одноклассники».finding: Odnoklassniki (ok.ru) is a Russian social network launched 26 March 2006 by Albert Popkov as a hobby project that deliberately imitated the American Classmates.com 'find former schoolmates' model; it was sold in 2008 to Yuri Milner's DST/Mail.ru Group and was VKontakte's principal domestic rival until VK overtook it in popularity in December 2008. The name literally means 'classmates' (people who studied in the same class), and for a Russian reader around 2013 it connoted the mainstream, family-oriented network for rediscovering old school friends — skewing older and more provincial than VKontakte's urban youth culture. In a Durov biography it functions as the contrast case: the rival VK was explicitly positioned against and ultimately overtook.
«Одноклассники».rationale: All three use the settled brand transcription rather than literal translation, preserving denotation fully; the zh Gloss '同学' (the simplified form of the name's literal meaning, matching Chinese Wikipedia) resolves the English-looking name into a clue a Chinese reader can parse, and ja uses the standard katakana アドナクラースニキ as fixed by the Japanese Wikipedia article, not the colleague's ad-hoc オドノクラスニキ. The sacrificed element is the schoolmates connotation in en/ja, which only survives in zh — an acceptable trade for an organization name.

«Ведомости».finding: «Ведомости» refers to the Moscow-based Russian-language business daily founded in 1999. Around 2013 it covered economics, finance, companies, and politics and was jointly owned by Sanoma Independent Media, the Financial Times, and The Wall Street Journal’s publisher, giving the name connotations of an authoritative, internationally backed business paper for professional and elite readers. It is not a generic reference to “news” or “reports.”
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/フィナンシャル・タイムズ

rendering.zh: 俄罗斯《韦多莫斯季》商业日报
rendering.ja: ロシア経済紙『ヴェドモスチ』

«Ведомости».rationale: The English keeps the established romanized masthead; the Chinese and Japanese add the business-newspaper category so readers retain its institutional weight and register. This sacrifices the Russian title’s literal meaning while avoiding the misleading Chinese title 《新闻报》, commonly liable to be confused with other Russian newspapers.

Кузя.finding: Кузя is a familiar diminutive of the Russian name Кузьма (Kuzma), derived from Кузнецов (Kuznetsov). In the context of Nikolai Kononov's 2012 book 'Код Дурова' (Durov's Code), it refers to an early VKontakte infrastructure programmer by the surname Kuznetsov, nicknamed Кузя by colleagues. The nickname carries the informal, affectionate register typical of Russian startup teams in the mid-2000s. Wikipedia does not have a dedicated article on this individual, and web searches did not surface an independent biography, so the identification rests on the book's context and the gloss provided. For a Russian reader circa 2013, Кузя would have been immediately recognized as a personal nickname, not a reference to a house-elf or cartoon character.
Кузя.rationale: Preserved denotation (the person's nickname) and the informal register by transliterating directly; sacrificed any attempt to explain the diminutive formation, which would require a footnote. In English and Japanese the transliteration is standard practice for Russian nicknames in biographical prose; in Chinese the phonetic rendering 库贾 is concise and avoids the association with 库兹 (which might evoke the house-elf 'Kreacher' or similar).

Цыплухин.finding: In the VK/Durov milieu of ~2011–13 the surname almost always points to Владислав (Влад) Цыплухин, long-time press secretary / head of PR at VKontakte, later a media operator (Coub, VC.ru/TJournal’s «Комитет»). English wire copy already spelled him Tsyplukhin. The brief’s «Ilya Tsypkin» and «School of Seduction» radio hero is not corroborated on Wikipedia; if the 2013 book uses that first name it is likely a mix-up or a different minor figure, but the Latin form still locks to Tsyplukhin.
Цыплухин.rationale: Kept the established English media spelling and the existing ja/zh phonetic calques; sacrificed a possible Ilya/Tsypkin variant because ru.wiki and NYT-era English both use Vladislav Tsyplukhin.

Мильнер.finding: Мильнер refers to Yuri Borisovich Milner (b. 1961), the Russian-born Israeli billionaire investor who co-founded Mail.ru Group (later renamed VK) and founded DST Global. In the context of a 2013 Durov/VKontakte biography, he is the key strategic investor whose DST stake was rolled into Mail.ru Group, making him a central figure in the company's ownership history. The Russian spelling with the soft sign (Мильнер) is standard and unambiguous in Russian-language sources.
Мильнер.rationale: All three renderings preserve denotation exactly: they are the established, canonical forms in each language's Wikipedia and press. No connotation or register is at stake for a surname; the only requirement is consistency with earlier chapters, which these standard forms guarantee.

Одноклассники.finding: Одноклассники (ok.ru) is a Russian social network launched in March 2006 by Albert Popkov, modeled on the US site Classmates.com. By 1 January 2013 it had over 205 million registered users and was the second-most popular social network in Russia, directly behind VKontakte and ahead of Facebook. In the context of a Durov biography it denotes VK's principal domestic rival for Russian-speaking users. All three non-Russian Wikipedia editions (English, Chinese, Japanese) use the Latin form 'Odnoklassniki' as the article title, treating it as an untranslatable brand name.
Одноклассники.rationale: All three target-language Wikipedia editions already use the Latin brand name 'Odnoklassniki' as their standard form, so denotation and brand recognition are fully preserved. The literal meaning ('classmates') is sacrificed in all three languages, but this is the correct trade-off for a proper-name brand in a business biography; a translated gloss would mislead readers into thinking it is a common noun rather than a company name.

Vi veri universum vivus vici.finding: A modern Latin motto (often abbreviated V.V.V.V.V.) meaning roughly 'By the power of truth, I, while living, have conquered the universe.' It is Aleister Crowley's A∴A∴ motto, later popularized by Alan Moore's V for Vendetta (and the 2005 film), where the character V wrongly ascribes it to Faust/Marlowe. Russian Wikipedia and 2010s Runet repeat that Faust attribution as a common misconception; Durov's gloss matches the usual Russian translation. For a 2013 Russian reader it signalled occult/anarchist-internet cool, not classical Latin.

rendering.en: Vi veri universum vivus vici — 'By the power of truth, I, living, have conquered the universe'
rendering.zh: Vi veri universum vivus vici（拉丁语：“我凭借真理之力，活着征服了宇宙”）
rendering.ja: Vi veri universum vivus vici（ラテン語：「真実の力によって、生ける我は宇宙を征服した」）

Vi veri universum vivus vici.rationale: Keep the Latin plus Durov's gloss in all three languages so Faust is neither added nor silently corrected; denotation of the motto is preserved, Crowley's/V-for-Vendetta subtext is left implicit.
